cards.headline: A price is just the last trade someone agreed to.
cards.body: Nobody sets a stock's price. A buyer and a seller met at $84.20, agreed, and that number became the price. The next trade may happen at $84.19 or at $85. The tape is a running record of agreements, not a verdict on the company.

art.alt: A buyer and a seller shake hands over a single price marker, above a running tape of past trades.

cards.headline: Supply and demand for the shares.
cards.body: A price moves when more money wants in than wants out, or the reverse. What gets bid on is the **shares** — a limited number of them. A fine company with no buyers today still falls today.

art.alt: Supply and demand curves crossing at the market price.

cards.title: Record profit, missed forecast
cards.caption: Northwind earned $1.30 a share — its best year ever, 18% above last year. Analysts had forecast $1.45. The stock fell 9% the next morning.

cards.headline: The price already contains what everyone expects.
cards.body: If the whole market expects $1.45, buyers have already paid up for $1.45. Delivering exactly $1.45 changes nothing. Only the gap between what was expected and what arrived is new information — and only new information moves a price.

art.alt: A reported result compared with the market expectation, with the difference marked as surprise.

cards.prompt: Harbor Foods reports the highest profit in its 40-year history. Analysts had expected slightly more. What is the most likely reaction in the stock that morning?

options.label: It rises — record profit is good news
It falls — the result missed forecasts

cards.explanation: Good news is not the same as **better than expected** news. The record profit was already paid for; the shortfall against forecasts was the only new fact. Reactions are never guaranteed, but the surprise is what gets traded.

cards.title: The week around an earnings report
cards.caption: The price drifted up all week as buyers positioned for a strong quarter. The quarter was strong. It just was not strong enough, and the gap closed in one session.

cards.body: Four things move expectations more than anything else. Watch what each one does to the forecast, not to the headline.
A stock does not move on good news or bad news. It moves on the gap between what happened and what the market already [[1]].
cards.explanation: Analysts publish estimates, and those estimates are already sitting inside today's price. The surprise, in either direction, is the only part that has to be repriced.

cards.summary: A price is the last agreement between a buyer and a seller, and it moves when expectations change — not when news is merely good.
bullets: Supply and demand for the shares set the price, not the company's merit.
Whatever the market already expects is built into today's price.
Record results can still send a stock down if forecasts were higher.
Earnings, guidance, rates, and sentiment all work by moving expectations.

art.alt: A market audience compares the performance it imagined with the different result revealed on stage.

cards.insight: The market does not pay for good news. It pays for news that is better than the news it already believed.
